ledger.note: 846: Adalbert I is granted the margraviate of Tuscany. Infobox 'Adalbert I granted margraviate: 846'; 'The march was a Carolingian creation, a successor of the Lombard Duchy of Tuscia'; the first margrave was Adalbert I, granted the title in 846; Florence's page: 'Since 846 AD, the city had been part of the Marquisate of Tuscany.' The page names cities and the Arno valley, not a boundary.

c. 1000: Pisa stands apart from the margraves. Infobox 'Established: c. 1000', 'Preceded by: March of Tuscany'; the marquis was 'the nominal feudal sovereign of Pisa' who 'had already been excluded from power' (undated). The year is the infobox's approximation.

1115: Florence rebels on Matilda's death. 'The republic originated in 1115, when the Florentine people rebelled against the Margraviate of Tuscany' (infobox 'First established: 1115', 'Preceded by: 1115: March of Tuscany'); the city 'did not submit readily to her successor' Rabodo (r. 1116-1119), killed in a dispute with the city. The page says it is not known precisely when the independent government formed.

1125: the Republic of Siena. 'The foundation of the Republic of Siena is traditionally dated to 1125'; infobox 'Preceded by: Bishop of Siena (within Tuscany); March of Tuscany; Republic of Massa' and 'Deposition of the bishop who ruled the city: 1125'. The page does not describe the relation to the margraves.

region.text: Lucca province, whose territories 'included the Garfagnana to the north'

ledger.note: 1160: Lucca buys its feudal rights from Welf VI. 'The city bought the feudal rights from Margrave Welf VI in 1160, hence became subject only to the emperors' (infobox 'Established: 1160'); Welf VI held the march 1152-1160 (March page). The Lucca page also has the city start 'to constitute itself an independent commune' after Matilda's death in 1115 and its administration acknowledged by Margrave Conrad in 1120.

1185: the margraves take Florence back. 'This prosperity was shattered when Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa invaded the Italian Peninsula in 1185. As a result, the margraves of Tuscany reacquired Florence and its townlands.' The page dates the invasion, not the reacquisition.
1197: Florence reasserts its independence. 'The Florentines reasserted their independence when Emperor Henry VI died in 1197.'

region.text: the remaining march: Arezzo, Pistoia, Volterra, Prato, Poggibonsi and the rest, 'splintered between the competing republics of Florence, Pisa, Siena, Arezzo, Pistoia and Lucca'

ledger.note: 1197: the Tuscan League. Infobox 'Formation of Tuscan League: 1197' (with papal backing) and 'Claimed by Papacy: 1198'; 'After this, Tuscany was splintered between the competing republics'. The page states no dissolution date; 1197 is the last infobox date before the papal claim.

wars.name: Florentine rising against the margraves
wars.outcome: The city 'did not submit readily' to Matilda's successor Rabodo (r. 1116-1119), 'who was killed in a dispute with the city'; the page says the death of Rabodo in 1119 'should be a turning point' and that the first official mention of the Florentine republic was in 1138, when several Tuscan cities formed a league against the then margrave.

wars.name: Barbarossa's invasion of Italy (1185) and the Florentine reconquest
wars.outcome: After Barbarossa's invasion in 1185 'the margraves of Tuscany reacquired Florence and its townlands'; the Florentines reasserted their independence when Emperor Henry VI died in 1197.

certainty.note: A margraviate of cities and counties with no frontier described on any page; the communes' contadi are the researcher's radii and provinces.

notes: No Cliopatria row: every keyframe is new. Start 846 is the infobox's grant to Adalbert I; the page also says the march grew from the Lombard Duchy of Tuscia after 773/74, so the Carolingian march may be older, and the page leaves its 'Established' field empty. End 1197 (Tuscan League, papal claim in 1198) is the last infobox date; Matilda's death in 1115 and the communes of 1115-1160 make the real margraviate shrink long before. The extent is the region Tuscany (86 cells) because the page lists cities, not borders; the south (Maremma, Grosseto) and Lunigiana are unproven. Pisa's independence is the infobox's c. 1000 and nothing else; Pisa's own dossier has the same date and no counterpart. Arezzo, Pistoia, Volterra, Prato and Poggibonsi, listed as successors on the page, have no dossier and no date on the pages opened; the remaining march is drawn to 1197 and then given to the communes without a counterpart. The kingdom-of-italy-medieval dossier (855-961) and middle-franks may need a matching loss for Tuscany. San Miniato as capital after 1116 is bridging. The ruler strip is left out: the page lists margraves (Adalbert I 846, the Bonifacii to 931, Matilda 1055-1115, Rabodo 1116-1119, Henry the Proud 1137-1139, Welf VI 1152-1160) but the reign years of the others were not read.
